concepts.name: Wave Mechanics and Coastal Erosion Processes
key_dimensions: Distinction between swash, backwash, and longshore drift and their erosional roles
Types of wave action: hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition, and corrosion — specific landforms each produces
Constructive vs. destructive waves: conditions, characteristics, and contrasting landforms formed
UPSC trap: why high-energy coasts erode while low-energy coasts deposit — conditions and exceptions

concepts.name: Sea Cliffs and Wave-Cut Platforms
key_dimensions: Step-by-step formation sequence: wave notch → overhang → cliff retreat → wave-cut platform
Factors controlling cliff morphology: rock type, dip angle, joint patterns, and wave energy
Wave-cut platform vs. wave-built terrace: formation mechanism and spatial relationship
UPSC trap: distinguishing wave-cut platform (erosional) from continental shelf (structural) — common confusion

concepts.name: Sea Caves, Arches, Stacks, and Stumps — Erosional Sequence
key_dimensions: Sequential formation: headland → cave → arch → stack → stump as a continuum of erosion
Role of joints, faults, and lithological weaknesses in initiating cave formation
Geo (narrow inlet) vs. blow hole: formation distinction and geographic examples
UPSC trap: stacks are erosional remnants, NOT depositional features — frequently misclassified

concepts.name: Beaches: Formation, Morphology, and Classification
key_dimensions: Beach profile components: berm, foreshore, backshore, and their dynamic equilibrium
Factors determining beach material size: wave energy, source rock, distance from source
Pocket beaches vs. barrier beaches: formation conditions and structural differences
UPSC trap: beaches are temporary, dynamic features — not permanent landforms; seasonal changes in profile

concepts.name: Spits, Bars, and Tombolos — Depositional Landforms
key_dimensions: Spit formation mechanism: longshore drift deflection at bay mouths or river mouths
Recurved/hooked spit vs. straight spit: role of refracted waves and tidal currents
Tombolo formation: how deposition connects an island to the mainland — examples (e.g., Mont Saint-Michel type)
UPSC trap: bar (fully closes a bay) vs. spit (one end attached) vs. tombolo (connects island) — definitional precision required

concepts.name: Barrier Islands and Lagoons
key_dimensions: Three competing theories of barrier island formation: submergence, longshore drift, offshore bar emergence
Lagoon formation and characteristics: Chilika Lake, Pulicat Lake as Indian examples
Barrier island vs. barrier reef vs. offshore bar: structural and formational distinctions
UPSC trap: Chilika classified as a lagoon (brackish, behind barrier spit) — not a lake in the strict geomorphological sense

concepts.name: Deltas: Types, Formation, and Controls
key_dimensions: Formation conditions: sediment supply > wave/tidal energy to remove sediment
Classification: arcuate (Nile), bird's foot (Mississippi), cuspate (Tiber), estuarine (Rhine) — distinguishing characteristics
Factors inhibiting delta formation: high tidal range, strong longshore drift, submarine canyons
UPSC trap: Ganga-Brahmaputra forms a delta while Indus forms an estuary — reasons and comparison

concepts.name: Estuaries vs. Deltas — Comparative Geomorphology
key_dimensions: Estuary formation: drowned river valleys where tidal energy exceeds sediment supply
Why some rivers form estuaries (Indus, Narmada, Tapti) vs. deltas (Ganga, Mahanadi, Krishna)
Role of tectonic setting: ria coasts (drowned valleys on passive margins) vs. delta coasts
UPSC trap: Narmada and Tapti flow into Gulf of Khambhat forming estuaries due to tectonic faulting — NOT deltas despite large discharge

concepts.name: Coral Reefs: Types, Formation Conditions, and Distribution
key_dimensions: Darwin's subsidence theory: fringing reef → barrier reef → atoll as sequential stages
Optimal conditions: water temperature (23–25°C), salinity (27–40 ppt), clear shallow water, sunlight
Fringing reef vs. barrier reef vs. atoll: structural differences and spatial relationship to landmass
UPSC trap: coral reefs absent on west coasts of continents due to cold upwelling currents — critical biogeographic exception

concepts.name: Atolls: Formation Theories and Geomorphic Significance
key_dimensions: Darwin's subsidence theory vs. Daly's glacial control theory — evidence for each
Reef flat, lagoon, and outer reef slope: morphological components and ecological roles
Indian Ocean atolls: Lakshadweep as a coral atoll vs. Andaman & Nicobar as continental island arc
UPSC trap: Lakshadweep (atoll origin, coral) ≠ Andaman & Nicobar (volcanic/tectonic origin) — frequently confused in questions

concepts.name: Mangroves: Geomorphic Role and Coastal Dynamics
key_dimensions: Geomorphic function: sediment trapping, coastline accretion, and wave energy dissipation
Conditions for mangrove growth: tropical/subtropical, sheltered coasts, tidal flats, saline-brackish water
Sundarbans mangrove: role in delta stabilization and its vulnerability to sea-level rise
UPSC trap: mangroves reduce coastal erosion but can also trap sediment causing channel shifts — dual geomorphic role

concepts.name: Coastal Dunes and Aeolian Processes at Shorelines
key_dimensions: Formation mechanism: onshore wind transports beach sand above high tide line
Foredune vs. parabolic dune vs. transgressive dune: morphology and stability differences
Role of vegetation (marram grass) in dune stabilization and its removal causing blow-outs
UPSC trap: coastal dunes are aeolian landforms occurring in coastal settings — NOT marine depositional features

concepts.name: Ria Coasts and Fiord Coasts — Submergent Coastlines
key_dimensions: Ria: drowned river valley, funnel-shaped, shallows inland — formed by eustatic sea-level rise
Fiord: drowned glacial trough, steep walls, overdeepened, sill at mouth — found in high latitudes
Ria vs. fiord: depth profile, origin (fluvial vs. glacial), and geographic distribution
UPSC trap: fiords have a characteristic shallow sill at the mouth (terminal moraine) despite great inland depths — causes stratification

concepts.name: Emergent Coastlines: Raised Beaches and Marine Terraces
key_dimensions: Formation: isostatic rebound (post-glacial) or tectonic uplift causing old wave-cut platforms to emerge
Raised beach: former beach deposits now above sea level — evidence of relative sea-level fall
Staircase terraces: multiple raised beaches indicating episodic uplift events
UPSC trap: raised beaches indicate emergent coasts (land rising OR sea falling) — both mechanisms can produce identical landforms

concepts.name: Longshore Drift and Its Landform Products
key_dimensions: Mechanism: oblique wave approach → swash moves material diagonally → backwash returns perpendicularly
Landforms produced: spits, bars, cuspate forelands, tombolos, and beach drift patterns
Human interference: groynes interrupt longshore drift causing updrift accumulation and downdrift starvation
UPSC trap: longshore drift direction is determined by prevailing wind direction, NOT coastline orientation — a common misconception

concepts.name: Sea Level Changes and Coastal Landform Responses
key_dimensions: Eustatic (global sea level) vs. isostatic (land level) changes — net relative sea-level change determines coastal response
Transgression (rising sea level) landforms: rias, fiords, lagoons vs. regression landforms: raised beaches, emerged platforms
Holocene sea-level rise and its role in shaping present Indian coastline — submergence of river valleys
UPSC trap: Scandinavia has falling relative sea levels (isostatic rebound) despite global sea-level rise — isostasy overrides eustasy locally

concepts.name: Coastal Geomorphology of India — Regional Patterns
key_dimensions: West coast (Malabar/Konkan): emergent, rocky, cliffed, estuaries — vs. East coast (Coromandel): submergent, sandy, deltaic, lagoons
Reason for contrast: Western Ghats proximity, tectonic history, river regimes, and sediment supply differences
Specific features: Backwaters of Kerala (lagoons), Chilika/Pulicat (lagoons), Lakshadweep (atolls), Gulf of Mannar reef
UPSC trap: India's west coast is erosional/rocky while east coast is depositional/sandy — opposite of what students intuitively expect

concepts.name: Tidal Flats, Mudflats, and Salt Marshes
key_dimensions: Formation: fine sediment deposition in low-energy, sheltered, intertidal zones with high tidal range
Succession sequence: mudflat → salt marsh → reclaimed land — role of pioneer vegetation (Spartina)
Ecological vs. geomorphic significance: carbon storage, nursery habitat, and coastal protection
UPSC trap: mudflats form in HIGH tidal range environments (macro-tidal) while beaches dominate LOW tidal range — tidal energy determines deposit type

concepts.name: Headlands and Bays — Differential Erosion and Coastal Straightening
key_dimensions: Formation: alternating resistant and weak rock bands perpendicular to coast → differential erosion
Wave refraction around headlands: energy concentration on headlands vs. energy dispersion in bays
Long-term coastal evolution: headlands erode, bays fill with sediment → coastline straightens over time
UPSC trap: wave energy is CONCENTRATED at headlands (causing erosion) and DISPERSED in bays (causing deposition) — students often reverse this

concepts.name: Coastal Erosion Hazards and Vulnerability — Geomorphic Perspective
key_dimensions: Factors controlling coastal erosion rate: rock resistance, wave energy, sea-level rise, human modification
Cliff recession rates and their measurement — soft rock cliffs (glacial till) vs. hard rock cliffs
Positive vs. negative sediment budget: how human structures (dams, seawalls) starve coasts of sediment
UPSC trap: seawalls protect the land behind them but accelerate erosion at their base and on adjacent unprotected coasts — coastal squeeze phenomenon
